t: Maximum Value of Concatenated Binary Segments
o:
Each segment is a run of 1s followed by a run of 0s. We reorder segments to maximize the resulting binary number. The classic comparator applies: place A before B iff the concatenation A+B exceeds B+A. Since both orders have the same total length, comparing A+B vs B+A numerically is equivalent to comparing them lexicographically as strings — so we can build the actual segment strings (total length ≤ 2e5) and sort with that comparator, then evaluate the value modulo 1e9+7.

Example 1: segments '10' and '11'; '11'+'10' = '1110' > '10'+'11' = '1011', so order ['11','10'] gives 14. Example 2: '111' then '1000' gives 1111000 = 120.
k: A+B vs B+A comparison is a valid total order here, and equal lengths make string comparison equivalent to numeric comparison.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort by pairwise concatenation comparator
a.i: Materialize each segment as a string, sort with cmp(a,b) = compare(a+b, b+a), concatenate, and fold the bits into the answer modulo 1e9+7. Transitivity of the 'a+b ≥ b+a' relation guarantees the sort is well-defined.
s: Sort with the comparator a+b > b+a.
Iterate bits of the joined string: ans = (ans*2 + bit) % MOD.
a.t: O(L log n) where L ≤ 2e5 is the total string length — building strings is linear, comparisons cost O(L) each across the sort

a.n: Approach 2: Comparator on (ones, zeros) without materializing strings
a.i: Segment A dominates B for placement first iff A·2^{|B|} + B > B·2^{|A|} + A, i.e., ones_A·(2^{z_B} − 1) > ones_B·(2^{z_A} − 1) after algebra on the run structure. Comparing via logarithms or big integers avoids building strings, which matters if total length were huge; with the given limits it is simply an alternative formulation.
s: Compare pairs using big-integer arithmetic: aBeforeB iff ones_a·(2^{zeros_b} − 1) > ones_b·(2^{zeros_a} − 1).
Sort, then fold value = Σ over segments of (value·2^{ones} + (2^{ones} − 1)) followed by multiplying by 2^{zeros}, all mod p.
a.t: O(n log n · C) where C is the cost of one big-number/log comparison — comparable to Approach 1 here

w: Use Approach 1: building strings is cheap under the stated total-length bound and the comparator is obviously correct. Pitfalls: forgetting that equal-length concatenations make lexicographic comparison valid, and modular evaluation order (fold bits left to right). Edge cases: segments that are all 1s or all 0s, and a single segment. Follow-up: minimize the value instead, or handle segments with mixed internal patterns (the generic a+b vs b+a comparator still applies).
